Largely limited by the volume of electrolyte used, lean electrolyte conditions (electrolyte/sulfur mass ratio <3) present enormous challenges that have led to very poor specific capacity and rate performance.
Previous studies have identified that the high concentration of polysulfide is responsible for the poor discharge voltage.
However, there still lacks sufficient understanding of the processes occurring at lean electrolyte conditions.

In this work we uncovered a polysulfide concentration regulating mechanism that operates through the precipitation and redissolution of solid sulfurbased species (reversibly precipitated sulfur species, RPSS).
This occurs in a concerted manner in a global sense through the cathode and can be measured using impedance spectroscopy.
It was found that the more RPSS that is formed, the higher the energy density of discharge.
We propose that high concentration of polysulfide tends to supersaturate, which impeded the formation of RPSS.

Employing an electrolyte with low Li ion concentration along with using poorly dissociating lithium salts allowed for more RPSS formation and ultimately enabled discharge at >2.0 V at 0.05 C, at E/S = 2.5, and at room temperature without the use of an engineered cathode. ■INTRODUCTION The lithium−sulfur battery is an attractive next-generation battery technology due to the natural abundancy of sulfur and high theoretical energy density.1−4 However, the practically achievable energy density (volumetric and gravimetric) is highly dependent on the volume/mass of electrolyte used.5,6 At relevant electrolyte conditions (electrolyte/sulfur mass ratio, E/S < 3),7 the cell experiences enormous overpotential that results in extremely poor rate performances (often well below 0.05 C).8,9 An increasingly popular and reasonably robust class of strategies centers around moving away from the traditional solid−liquid−solid conversion of a lithium−sulfur battery to a solid−solid conversion.

This is achieved by either employing sparingly soluble electrolytes10,11 and/or covalently-bonded sulfur polymer.12−14 With almost every aspect of this class of strategies appealing, its most undermining property is the intrinsically lower operating potentials due to a fundamental change in the reaction pathways.15 A study by Eroglu et al. presented a rapid decline in projected pack-level energy density when the cell-level voltage is <2.0 V.16−18 Since the operating voltage of lithium−sulfur batteries hovers around 2.0−2.2 V, the pack level energy density of the lithium−sulfur battery is particularly sensitive to any decrease/increase of cell voltage.
A low cell voltage can drastically increase the number of cells required to reach often pre-established device-level operating voltages.
This would effectively increase the mass of “deadweight” components such as current collectors, electrolyte, etc., that do not scale well even with a high single-cell-level energy density.
While the solid−solid-based systems can reach the necessary lean electrolyte conditions, they are typically operated at a much lower average cell voltage i.e., ∼1.5 V.

As part of a long list of requirements for commercial success, maintaining a >2.0 V average discharge voltage while also operating at an appreciable current density, room temperature, high sulfur loading, and all under lean electrolyte conditions (≤3.0 μL mgs) remains to be a monumental task.
Many alternative strategies have been explored to achieve a low E/S ratio while still maintaining a solid−liquid−solid conversion mechanism.

These include the use of macroporous carbon that assists in temporarily relieving the overpotential by allowing more local electrolyte access and slowing the onset of large overpotential;19,20 the use of polysulfide adsorptive binders can be useful in taking polysulfide out of the bulk solution to lower the overall impedance but still lacks significant progress.21 Increasing the solubility of polysulfide has also been a very popular direction of study.

solution and S3-radical formation have led to some success in improving the specific discharge capacity.
However, these solvents tend to have a high viscosity and are also incompatible with Li metal.

The reduction in the concentration of Li ion salt has also been pursued, where the proportion of free solvents are increased.25 It was suggested that this increases the solubility of polysulfide by the common-ion effect, which, in turn, reduces the overpotentials.
Improvements in discharge capacity and voltage were observed but only at a relatively high E/S ratio of 5.

Very lean electrolyte conditions (E/S ratio of ≤2.5 μL mgs) were also achieved with various techniques but were either discharged at very low current densities (<0.0025 C with 1 C = 1675 mA g−1),14,26 centered around highly airsensitive materials,27 or required elevated temperature (55 °C)28 to function at >2.0 V.
The large overpotential often observed at the LEC usually manifests itself as a large dip at the onset of the second discharge plateau.

This has been termed the Li2S nucleation overpotential.29 A particularly troublesome property of this dip is its tendency to chronically persists for the remainder of the second discharge plateau, i.e., cell voltage never recovers.
This leads to average cell voltages well below 2.0 V.
The cause for the overpotential can be reliably traced to increases in the charge transfer resistance.
However, this is still a rather ambiguous source of overpotential that can be caused by many cathode processes.
These include poor polysulfide mass transfer limitations (from high viscosity),30 polysulfide clustering/gelation,31,32 passivation of conductive surfaces,19 or a combination thereof.
Deconvolution of these sources of high overpotential is a difficult task that might also lead to varying conclusions depending on the specific LSB cell system studied.
Accordingly, it is difficult to devise effective strategies for LSB operation under LEC.
It might be instructive to study the underlying processes that are occurring in configurations that have been already shown to allow for relatively higher performing LEC-LSB.
There exist clear configurations19 where cell at LEC experienced large overpotential at the onset of the second discharge plateau but can reliably recover its potential.
Accordingly, there must exist some type of mechanism at the cathode that can help the cell recover from the voltage dip and avoid a chronically depressed discharge.

In this work, we uncover a polysulfide concentration regulating mechanism that exists under lean electrolyte conditions in a traditional solid−liquid−solid conversion type LSB by employing operando and relaxation-based electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) analysis.

We discovered a strong relationship between the interfacial resistance (high frequency semicircle, centered at ∼103−105 Hz) at a specific depth of discharge (DOD) and the discharge material level energy density.
Cells with more than one interfacial resistance increasing event as a function of DOD and larger magnitude of such an event were found to deliver higher discharge energy density.
We attributed this to sulfur-based species that are reversibly deposited as deduced from a relaxation-based EIS study where changes in the phase angle were tracked.
The formation and importance of reversibly precipitated sulfur species (RPSS) are discussed.
Promotion of RPSS formation led to significant improvements in cell potential and capacity.

Using a highly Li ion deficient electrolyte with poorly dissociating anion and a standard “nonengineered” sulfur electrode based on commercially available micrometer-sized sulfur particles at 3.5 mg cm−2 (60% sulfur content), we were able to achieve a high discharge specific capacity (∼850 mAh g−1) with an E/S ratio of 2.5 μL mg−1 at a rate of 0.05 C (1 C = 1675 mA g−1), at room temperature, and with a second plateau well above 2.0 V. ■RESULTS AND DISCUSSION The poor performance of lean electrolyte conditions (LECs) during a single discharge can be succinctly described by two important deficiencies associated with the discharge process: (1) the existence of a large overpotential/nucleation “dip” and (2) a chronically depressed discharge potential following the dip.
The potential of the dip often determines whether the cell can proceed into the second discharge plateau (depending on the cutoff voltage).
In the case where the cell can sustain a second discharge plateau, the depressed discharge potential determines the operating voltage and energy density of the cell.

related to the high polysulfide concentration.
The large potential dip that occurs before the onset of the second discharge voltage plateau is where the polysulfide concentration is expected to be at its highest.

Conventional understanding dictates that when the polysulfide concentration increases, the viscosity and corresponding electrolyte resistance increase, slowed polysulfide/Li+ transport from bulk to surfaces,30 or a clustering/gelation effect of high concentration polysulfide,31−35 reducing the reaction kinetics.

Interestingly, while a some studies have reported a near full recovery of discharge potential after the initial potential dip,19 most studies found that the second discharge voltage plateau in continuously depressed/severely sloped.

This is clearly exemplified in Figure 1a, where a conventional 1 M lithium bis- (trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) and 0.25 M lithium nitrate (LiNO3) in a 1:1 by volume blend of 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) and 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) was used as electrolyte.
A clear voltage depression is present throughout the course of the second discharge plateau.

In principle, as the cell discharges, the polysulfide mass should be converted to insoluble species (Li2S/Li2S2), and thus, the global concentration of polysulfide (averaged across the entire electrolyte volume) should decrease.
Shown in Figure 1b, an “effective E/S ratio” was estimated as the reciprocal of the expected amount of sulfur mass remaining in solution and plotted against the depth of discharge.
It was assumed that all sulfur species were consumed to form either insoluble Li2S or soluble Li2S2.
As one discharges past the second plateau, the polysulfide concentration decreases and the “effective E/S ratio” increases.

If Li2S2 is the main discharge product, at ∼450 mAh g−1, the cell is expected to have a global polysulfide concentration that is similar to the highest solvated sulfur concentration experienced in an “equivalent cell” with an injected E/S ratio of 5 μL mg−1.
If Li2S is considered as the main product, the cell reaches an effective E/S ratio of 5 μL mg−1 at ∼700 mAh g−1.

Based on literature reports, a cell with an E/S ratio of ∼5 μL mg−1 can be expected to run relatively unhindered at 0.1 C even when using a relatively routine carbon nanotube/sulfur composite.36 Accordingly, a decrease in sulfur content in the electrolyte from discharging should impart some relief to any high polysulfide-concentrationderived overpotentials experienced by the cell.
Yet, this is often not observed with the chronic voltage depression persisting well into the second plateau and often never recovering at all.

Therefore, it appears that it is not the high concentration of polysulfide that is directly responsible for the chronically depressed second plateau under LEC, but some long-lasting negative effect that is caused by the mere temporary existence of a high polysulfide concentration.
This chronic lack of recovery in overpotential can be clearly demonstrated from operando electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) analysis over the course of discharge.
A series of operando EIS measurements were performed on cells using different Li salts and at varying concentrations.

A highly depressed discharge profile is observed during operando EIS (Figure 2a) employing an E/S ratio of 2.5 μL mgs −1 (using a standard electrolyte composition: 1 M LiTFSI and 0.25 M LiNO3 in DOL/DME 1:1 v/v) and a sulfur loading of 3.5 mgs cm−2.
Similar to the profile in Figure 1a, the cell was unable to recover the overpotential experienced during the dip, and in fact, the impedance continuously increased.
The fitted impedance values are shown in Figure 2b as a function of the discharge time.

Re and Rint peaked at the onset of the second discharge plateau, which is consistent with literature.37 Like the flooded conditions, the peak in Re likely is a gauge of the viscosity of the electrolyte.
Further confirming previous reports,21,31 Rct is by far the largest impedance contribution in the cell under LEC.

In the case of low Li ion composition, Re peaked at ∼100 ohm, nearly triple that of the high concentration electrolyte.

The cause of this surprising result is unclear, but we suspect that the use of a lower Li ion concentration increased the concentration of dissolved polysulfide, which might have caused an increase in the viscosity.
Rint followed a similar trend for both high and low Li ion concentrations before the second discharge plateau.
However, a large increase in Rint was observed for the low Li ion electrolyte over the course of the second plateau, which we will discuss later.
In terms of magnitude, Rct represented the largest difference between the low (<500 ohm) and high Li ion (>2000 ohm) compositions.
Interestingly, the value of Rct for both electrolyte compositions reached nearly the same value when Re is at its maximum (commonly termed the high concentration of polysulfide in the system37).

Afterward, the Rct increased rapidly for the high Li ion composition while the Rct for the low Li ion composition only increased moderately and actually decreased after ∼4 h of operando EIS before reaching a plateau.
Clearly the low Li ion composition is an example of an electrolyte system that can recover from the large overpotential.
Both high and low Li ion concentration cells were able to enter into the second discharge plateau with a voltage of 1.98−1.97 V.
However, the higher Li ion concentration cell continued to drop in voltage, while the low Li ion concentration cell was able to maintain a stable voltage.

The ability of the low Li ion concentration cell to avoid a continued voltage drop is an indication that there must exist some mechanism for the cell to manage and regulate the high concentration of polysulfide.
To investigate such a regulation mechanism, we look toward understanding the surface condition of the cell at various depths of discharge (DOD) by observing the relaxation processes.

As the viscosity and polysulfide concentration are expected to be very high under LEC, we suspect that much of the diffusional and dissolutionbased relaxation processes (that can be used to infer the surface conditions of the cathode) occur over long time scales and even though the cell appears to have to have reached equilibrium.

To uncover the relaxation processes occurring at slower time scales, cells discharged to four different DOD were rested at OCV while their impedance was sampled intermittently (Kramers−Kronig analysis was employed to confirm that the EIS spectra were causal, Figure S1).

Four different DODs were selected and defined as follows: DOD-1: discharged to 8 h, Figures 3a−c; DOD-2: discharged to 9 h, Figures 3d−f; DOD-3: discharged to 11 h, Figures 3g−i; DOD-4: discharged to 13 h,Figures 3j−l.
Confirming our suspicions, the impedance elements changed significantly in magnitude even when rested at OCV.

As the impedance metrics tended to decrease (beside Rint), it cannot be due to the Li metal corrosion which tends to increase linearly with t0.5.38,39 Therefore, the relaxations are likely cathode-based processes.
Moreover, the relaxation trends change dramatically from DOD-1 to DOD-2 to DOD-3 with DOD-4 being relatively like DOD-3.
This means that conditions (surfaces, electrolyte composition) of the cell prior to rest vary significantly as a function of DOD.
Generally, across all DODs, Rint tended to decrease monotonically over time while Re tended to increase monotonically.
The most interesting phenomenon lies in Rct, which exhibited a rather surprising nonmonotonic trend for the cell rested from DOD- 1.
Right after the current was halted, Rct increased for a few hours, followed by a sharp decrease.
If discharge was halted at DOD-2, Rct initially held constant for a period of ∼2 h followed by a monotonic decrease.

Changes in Rct can be interpreted as a surface area change or polysulfide concentration change (Figure S2).
To delineate which one of these is dominating, we refer to the transient behavior of the Bode-phase plots during relaxation.
The peak position in the Bode-phase plots can be used as an indication of the characteristic frequency (fct) of the observed process.

A change in Rct caused by a process dominated by polysulfide concentration variations should experience a change in its fct, whereas a change in Rct dominated by surface area variations will tend to maintain a constant frequency peak position.
This can be rationalized if we first approximate the time constant of these processes as τ = RctC, where τ is the time constant (1/fct) and C is the capacitance.

Since capacitance C is proportional to the surface area and Rct is inversely proportional to the surface area, together, the impact of any surface area change will be likely nullified as they cancel each other.35,40 In other words, a decrease in Rct without any frequency change can be interpreted as a process mostly caused by an increase in the electronically active surface area.
On the other hand, a change in polysulfide concentration is not directly proportional to capacitance, which would be reflected in a change in τ.

Accordingly, a decrease in Rct accompanied by a change in τ can be interpreted as a phenomenon mostly dominated by an increase in concentration of redox active species, i.e., polysulfide concentration.
Using this analysis, we can deduce the events occurring during relaxation.
At DOD-1 (8 h of discharge, Figure 3a), the phase-peak associated with Rct (∼102 Hz) initially shifts to a lower frequency.
Once Rct stops increasing and begins to decrease, the frequency stops shifting and begins to maintain a constant value of ∼30 Hz.

This suggests that during the initial 3 h of relaxation, Rct increases due to a decrease in near-surface polysulfide concentration (likely diffusion to the bulk electrolyte) as illustrated in Figure 4a,b, whereas the subsequent decrease in Rct can be interpreted as an exposure of more surface area (Figure 4c).
As DOD-1 is at the early stages of the second discharge plateau, there likely exists a very high nearsurface polysulfide concentration.
Upon resting, the polysulfide surface concentration dissipates into the bulk electrolyte, decreasing the exchange current and increasing the Rct.

This suggests that there exist some solid precipitates of polysulfide that can redissolve when the nearsurface polysulfide concentration decreases.
We will refer to these as reversibly precipitated sulfur species (RPSS).

Cells that were discharged for longer durations (DOD-3 and DOD- 4) appear to only possess a decreasing Rct trend without change in fct (i.e., dominated by the surface area increase, Figures 3i and 3l, respectively).

This is again likely due to exposure of additional surfaces from the dissolution of RPSS, suggesting a polysulfide concentration below the solubility limit at the surface when discharged to DOD-3 and DOD-4 (as schematically shown in Figure 4f).
When the cell was halted at DOD-2 and rested, Rct initially maintains a constant value over 2 h of relaxation before proceeding to decrease rapidly akin to the other three DODs.

The initially constant value of Rct is likely an indication of the onset of redissolution, where the polysulfide concentration is at the solubility limit of RPSS, with a rather small driving force for dissolution.
As discharge progressed from DOD-1 to DOD-2, more polysulfide in solution is converted into insoluble Li2S/Li2S2.
This decreases the near-surface concentration of the polysulfide.

Further discharge to DOD-3 and DOD-4 likely resulted in a sufficiently low polysulfide concentration that enabled the substantial dissolution of RPSS essentially right after the galvanostatic discharge is halted.
DOD-2 appears to represent a turning point between a nearsurface polysulfide concentration that is too high for RPSS dissolution and a concentration low enough to begin redissolving RPSS.
Intriguingly, the discharge percentage of DOD-2 aligns nicely with features pertaining to how Rint evolves over the course of discharge.

Looking at the impedance vs DOD evolution for the high Li ion concentration electrolyte (Figure 2b), Rint was found to increase up to ∼60 ohm (denoted as Rint‐P1, peak 1 of Rint), followed by a decrease to ∼27 ohm, which then increases back up to ∼37 ohm (denoted as Rint‐P2, peak 2 of Rint).
There seem to be multiple Rint increasing/decreasing events, which we refer to as oscillations.

Similar trends were reported in another study but not discussed.21 As a confirmation, this oscillating trend of Rint vs DOD can even be seen without the assistance of equivalent circuit modeling; the existence of Rint‐P2 can be observed directly on the Nyquist plot (Figure S3).

More importantly, while the first peak of Rint is relatively similar between the high and low Li ion concentrations (∼61 and ∼57 ohm, respectively), there appears to exist a much larger difference in the second Rint peak (∼67 vs ∼35 ohm, respectively).
Overall, this potentially indicates a degree of importance to the level of Rint and RPSS as surface films.
From Figure 3a,d,g,j), we can also associate DOD-1 as before Rint‐P2, DOD-2 is near Rint‐P2, and DOD-3 and -4 are post Rint‐P2.
We postulate that the phenomenon that is responsible for the differing relaxation characteristics among the 4 DODs can be tracked by Rint.
With a magnitude comparatively lower than that of Rct, Rint has been rarely discussed even though it has important implications on the surface processes in the cathode.
The interpretation of Rint has been rather complex.
Miller et al.41 attempted deconvolution of the high- to mid-frequency regime using distribution of relaxation time analysis.
In their study, four distinct time constants were identified in the frequency regime typically considered Rint (103−106 Hz).
This was done by using a regularization parameter of 10−4.
Only one of the four time constants was found to match that of a Li/Li symmetric cell, i.e., the solid electrolyte interphase impedance.

Using a series of symmetric cells containing various combinations of sulfur cathodes, carbon-only electrode, and lithium polysulfide-containing electrolytes, the other three time constants were all assigned to cathode processes: interparticle resistance, double layer relaxation, and sulfur-based reactions.
All such cathode processes can be affected by the formation of insulating sulfur-based surface layers, suggesting Rint can be used as a probe for the cathode’s surface impedance.
We propose in the case of LEC, the main contribution of Rint is dominated by surface films in the form of RPSS.

More importantly, the RPSS does not form randomly and sporadically over the course of the second discharge plateau, but more concerted and oscillating in magnitude across different DODs.
To further understand the importance of Rint, a series of cells with different electrolyte compositions (Table S1) were subjected to the same in operando EIS analysis collected in Figure 2.

Since LEC negatively affects both the discharge capacity and potential, we utilized the active material level energy density (Wh kgs −1) as the main performance metric of interest to correlate against the impedance contributions in the cell.
As expected, the energy delivered by the first discharge appears to show a reasonably strong negative correlation with the Rct magnitude taken at 6 h of discharge.
The higher the observed Rct, the lower the energy density of the first discharge (Figure 5a).
It should be noted that 6 h was chosen as the representative Rct because it was roughly at 50% DOD in all cases.
No significant correlation was found between the electrolyte resistance (Re) peak near the end of the first discharge plateau and the energy of the cell as shown in Figure S4a.

This is somewhat unexpected given its known dependence on the polysulfide concentration43 and suggests that a high viscosity of the electrolyte stemming from polysulfide dissolution might not be a great sole predictor of performance.
From initial inspection, no correlation was observed between Rint‐P2 and Rint‐P1 with the energy density (Figures S4b and S4c, respectively).
However, we found that the ratio between the second and first Rint peak (Rint‐P2/Rint‐P1, Figure 5b) correlated rather strongly (R2 = 0.98) with the discharge energy density up to a ratio of ∼1.
After Rint‐P2 reaches a similar magnitude as Rint‐P2, it appears that the energy density decreases and does not change and becomes unrelated to the Rint peak ratio.
We speculate that perhaps there exists a minimum threshold value of Rint‐p2 for the cell to produce a high energy density.
This finding is surprising first because a higher impedance generally does not yield higher energy density and second, the magnitude of Rint is rather small in comparison to Rct.

Although Rint makes little contribution to the total impedance, from our relaxation experiments (Figure 3), Rint can be considered as a probe for the surface condition of the sulfur cathode, which then has a strong impact on the charge transfer resistance.

Furthermore, as the trend appears only after normalizing Rint‐P2 by Rint‐P1, the degree of the second surface film formation event is important only in relation to the first surface film formation event.
Cells with a higher Rint‐P2/Rint‐P1 performed better, indicating that the precipitation of these solid-sulfur species likely help to alleviate the high concentration of the cell discharged under LEC.

These interim solid sulfur-based species give the electrolyte a “mass sink” to temporarily store the polysulfide content as some form of RPSS (Figure 5c) This mechanism ultimately provides the cell with an alternative pathway to rapidly regulate the polysulfide concentration without relying on the slow kinetics of lithiating a high concentration of polysulfide into solid Li2S/Li2S2.

Consequently, cells that do not have a high Rint,P2 (when normalized to Rint,P1) are unable to form such redissolvable species (i.e., RPSS) and unable to eliminate/avoid the sources (clustering/aggregates/gelation) of chronic overpotentials.
In order to promote more formation of RPSS, we must first understand how they are limited.
It is known that lithium polysulfide tends to form clusters at high concentrations or low temperature.44 It is possible that such clusters cannot form RPSSs and are very stable.
One possible explanation is that the more stable the clusters, the higher the degree of supersaturation and the poorer its ability to precipitate out as an RPSS.
This is especially true for polymeric species.

Clusters/ aggregates in solution have been previously shown to substantially increases the solubility of a polymer.45 In contrast, electrolytes with less stable polysulfide clusters will tend to precipitate out of solution readily, forming the desired RPSSs.
To show this is the case, we investigated the stability of the polysulfide/electrolyte solution to temperature.
Upon cooling, the solubility of the polysulfide is expected to decrease, which should cause precipitation.
Polysulfides were mixed with electrolyte at high and low Li ion salt concentrations and studied using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC).

Because of the high polysulfide concentration, a slight compositional change from evaporation of DOL/DME (high vapor pressure at room temperature) could induce premature precipitation prior to testing, nullifying the results of the experiment.
The solvent was therefore switched to tetraglyme (TEGDME), which has a much lower vapor pressure.

DSC shows that cooling of high concentration polysulfide (8 mols L−1 nominally in the form of Li2S8) in an electrolyte solution of 1 M LiTFSI and 0.25 M LiNO3 in TEGDME did not produce any exotherms (Figure 6a,b).
When the Li ion concentration was lowered, a clear exothermic peak was found with an abrupt increase, characteristic of supersaturation.
We attribute this peak to the precipitation of Figure 6.

Samples without polysulfides (Figure S7) clearly exhibited TEGDME freezing endotherms at both high and low Li ion concentrations.
Evidently, the addition of polysulfide also impacted the freezing of the TEGDME, which further indicates a strong interaction between the polysulfide and TEGDME molecules stabilizing the solution.

A corollary of such a finding is that a stronger interaction between solvent and lithium polysulfide and lithium salts could provide an unwanted stabilizing effect of polysulfide clusters in solution during discharge.

This is likely detrimental to LEC LSB, which is in contrast to the common notion of increasing the solubility limit of polysulfide by using more polar solvents.23,46 Stronger solvating solvents will tend to interact more strongly with polysulfide and Li ions.

As expected, when solvents with higher solvating power such as 1,3-dimethyl-2- imidazolidinone, hexamethylphosphoramide, or dimethylacetamide were used at E/S of 2.5 μL mgs −1, no notable performance improvement was observed (Figure S8).
Arguably, the performance was slightly worse.

However, in flooded cells, where the concentration regime of polysulfide is much lower, notable performance enhancements have indeed been previously reported.47 From our results, the problem of lean E/S ratio (high concentration of polysulfide) does not depend on merely the solubility but is more related to the existing concentration of polysulfide in the electrolyte and the proclivity of aggregation/ clustering.
If clusters are formed, a higher polysulfide concentration can be achieved but might cause a higher charge transfer resistance.
Such clustering of polysulfide limits the formation of RPSSs and the polysulfide concentration cannot be regulated or remedied over the course of discharge.
When polysulfides are not stabilized in solution by clustering, RPSSs can form, acting as a temporary “mass sink” for the electrolyte to help mediate the polysulfide concentration.
Manthiram et al. have previously discussed that at low temperatures,44 polysulfides tend to form overpotentialinducing aggregates and found that using high donor anion salts could be beneficial.

Poorly dissociated Li salts could disrupt the formation of these lithium polysulfide clusters, as a significant portion of Li ions are already paired with their original anion and cannot participate in cluster formation.

With non-Li salts and high donor number anions, they were able to achieve an E/S ratio of 4 μL mgs −1.48 Zhang et al. described the possibility that cationic polysulfides (over-lithiated) are formed that hinder the discharge process.

It was proposed that a decrease in Li ion concentration will benefit the performance, citing an increased discharge capacity when using an E/S ratio of 3.5 μL mgs −1.49 At a very lean E/S ratio of <3.0 μL mgs −1, we observe that lowering Li ion concentration still exhibits a large overpotential.
Figure 7a shows the discharge voltage profile when an E/S ratio of 2.5 μL mgs −1 was used at a loading of 3.5 mg cm−2.
On the first and second cycles, these cells tend to produce unstable and ill-defined voltage plateaus at 0.05 C.
Notably, there is significant difference between the performance in Figure 7a and Figure S4i (operando EIS) even though they possessed similar concentrations.
This is likely due to the beneficial impact of the resting step throughout the operando EIS discharge.
Nevertheless, the discharge voltages in both cases are <2.0 V.

However, we found that the addition of lithium salt with high donor number anion (triflate) and under Li ion-starved conditions yielded a synergistic effect that substantially reduced the overpotential (Figure 7b) to a satisfactory voltage of well >2.0 V (albeit at 0.05 C).

Cathodic linear sweep voltammetry (Figure S9) using sulfur cathode at 3.5 mg cm−2 as the working electrode and Li metal as the reference/counter electrode at an E/S ratio of 2.5 also supports this conclusion.
When the typical electrolyte salt composition of 1 M LiTFSI and 0.25 M LiNO3 was used, only a weak reduction peak was observed.
The second peak was not observed likely to the poor kinetics of the reduction process under Li ion-rich conditions, which corroborates nicely with the galvanostatic discharge (Figure 2a).

However, when the Li ion content was reduced to 0.05 M LiTFSI and 0.025 M LiNO3, we begin to observe two distinct peaks (∼2.25 and ∼1.95 V), indicating a better ability of the cell to reduce sulfur polysulfide and also to reduce polysulfides to Li2S/Li2S2.
The peaks further become clearer and more distinct when 0.015 M LiTF is added to the electrolyte composition, yielding a higher peak current density.
We attribute this to the ability to form more RPSS as the lack of free Li ions limits the formation of stabilized polysulfide aggregates.
It should be noted that Li ion diffusion can also substantially influence the discharge.
One might suggest that the addition of LiTF could disrupt the polysulfide clustering and significantly increase the diffusion coefficient of the Li ions, causing the observed impact in performance.

The diffusion coefficient drops with increasing polysulfide concentration, which is expected due to increases in viscosity and clustering.
Interestingly, even with the same polysulfide concentrations, there are substantial differences between the three electrolyte compositions tested, indicating the importance of Li ion concentration.

At an E/S ratio of 2.5, the cell was unable to enter the second discharge plateau under a higher rate of 0.1 C.
However, at a slightly higher E/S ratio of 3 μL mgs −1, we varied the discharge rate from 0.05 to 0.2 C with an E/S ratio of 3 μL mgs −1 (Figure S12).

At 0.2 C the cell once again cannot enter the second discharge plateau with a cutoff voltage of 1.5 V.
Nevertheless, there still appears to be substantial benefit over just using low Li ion concentration composition (Figure 7a).
The triflate salt seemed to have a trade-off and yielded a decreased capacity.

The use of another high donor number salt, 0.375 M of lithium nitrate without LiTFSI (Figure S4e,h,j), also resulted in improved discharge profile over the standard 1 M LiTFSI + 0.25 M LiNO3 electrolyte.
While the voltage of 0.375 M LiNO3 (Figure S4e,h,j vs Figure S4c) was lower than that of Li ion-starved + high donor number salt (Figure 7c), the total capacity was higher for 0.375 M LiNO3.

The discharge voltage plateaus using our strategy is markedly higher than that of similar E/S ratio studies employing fluorinated solvents which tends to depress the discharge voltage.14 Directly increasing the LiTF while maintaining a higher Li ion concentration also yielded a higher voltage, but there still a depression in the discharge profile <2.0 V after the first cycle (Figure S13).

Overall, there appears to be some dependency of the discharge energy density (product of voltage and specific capacity) with the type of anion used and concentration of the salt, especially at the LEC regimes, and should be investigated in future studies.
Finally, we note that the use of low Li ion concentration electrolytes might lead to problems such as the lowered Li ion conductivity in the electrolyte.
While this might be partially alleviated by the dissolution of lithium polysulfides, it is unlikely to be sustainable at high current densities and near low and high SOCs.
Furthermore, use of low amounts of LiNO3 is likely to hinder cyclability as the Li metal will be less passivated against polysulfide shuttling.
This is evidenced by the short cycle life, where we observed stable cycling for only 9 cycles (Figure S14).

It is foreseeable that a combination of sulfophillic surfaces,51,52 salts with poorly dissociating anions, and moderately lowered Li ion concentration can provide significant improvements in performance at LEC and can be the topic future investigations. ■CONCLUSION Lean electrolyte conditions and high sulfur loading along with a cell-level discharge voltage >2.0 V are critical for achieving a commercially relevant lithium−sulfur battery.
Decreasing the E/S ratio to 2.5 can have a drastic influence on the cell that typically either prevents discharge entirely or produces a discharge profile that is very unstable and depressed.

While the existence of intermediate passivating films has been previously acknowledged in lithium−sulfur batteries,53 our findings suggest a seemingly concerted nature in this process and that the precipitated intermediate can be redissolved back.
Furthermore, it seems that the higher the magnitude of this process (taken as the Rint, mid-frequency impedance), the higher the discharge energy density.
We propose that these reversibly precipitated sulfur species (RPSS) in fact serve as a beneficial mass sink for temporarily storing polysulfide and transferring it out of the electrolyte solution.
Ultimately, this serves as a means for the cell to regulate the polysulfide concentration, reducing high polysulfide concentration-induced overpotentials.
High concentration polysulfide solutions that are too stable against precipitations are likely the cause of the poor performance observed at LEC.

It was found that the addition of lithium salts with high donor number salts in addition to an overall decrease in Li ions can promote formation of RPSS as deduced from the large Rint‐P2/Rint‐P1 ratio and increase the discharge energy density while maintaining an operating voltage of >2.0 V at room temperature and at 0.05 C. ■EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Materials.
